Sperm function

Many semen-exposure studies report short-term gains in motility or mitochondrial measures, but responses vary and some exposures are null or harmful. Livestock field results differ by species and breed, and human conception or live-birth benefit has not been established.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Many semen-exposure studies report short-term gains in motility or mitochondrial measures, but responses vary and some exposures are null or harmful. Livestock field results differ by species and breed, and human conception or live-birth benefit has not been established.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact sperm category contains 66 records: 58 experimental publications, four narrative reviews, one systematic review, one editorial or letter, one simulation, and one survey. The reviews reuse primary studies, and overlap between semen samples is not always clear, so the publication count is not a count of independent patient cohorts. The experimental records include 51 in-vitro or ex-vivo studies and seven animal-coded papers; one field study of irradiated boar semen is coded as ex-vivo semen but also reports sow outcomes.

Human and clinical evidence

Human-semen experiments frequently report short-term increases in progressive motility, swimming speed, viability, or mitochondrial activity. For example, a 633-nm red-light study increased sperm motility without detecting more oxidative DNA damage under its tested exposure (Preece et al., 2017, PubMed). These are laboratory measurements after semen exposure. No controlled human trial was identified showing that directly irradiating semen increases conception or live birth. Laser acupuncture studies have a different route of treatment and cannot be treated as trials of irradiated semen.

A broader 2023 systematic review of male-infertility PBM included 14 semen-exposure studies and one clinical trial of laser acupuncture. The acupuncture trial uses a different treatment route from irradiating semen, so it does not establish human fertility benefit from semen photobiomodulation (Eghbaldoost et al., 2023, PubMed).

Animal evidence

Mouse studies of heat- or chemotherapy-related testicular injury often report higher sperm counts or improved tissue and hormone measures after PBM. Livestock studies are not uniform: a 2021 field study using red-light-treated boar semen found no difference in pregnancy, farrowing, or litter outcomes in 2,955 Iberian sows, while a later 1,499-sow study reported higher pregnancy and delivery rates and larger litters in Large White and Yorkshire groups, but not consistently across breeds. A ram study after testicular heat injury found no improvement in semen quality. These results depend on species, breed, semen handling, and protocol (Crespo et al., 2021, PubMed; Sun et al., 2026, PubMed).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

A systematic review of 63 papers found that most reported a positive motility effect, while also describing major gaps in protocol and parameter reporting (Moradi et al., 2024, PubMed). Individual studies show why effects cannot be generalized: red or near-infrared exposures sometimes increased motility and ATP, whereas one human-sperm experiment using a broad near-infrared lamp reported lower viability and increased lipid peroxidation. The direction and size of response therefore depend on the light exposure and sample conditions.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The literature includes visible red light around 633–660 nm, visible blue light near 470 nm, and near-infrared light around 810–850 nm. A human-semen study reported 633-nm red light at 5.66 mW/cm² for 35 minutes; other experiments used fluences ranging from fractions of a joule to several joules per square centimetre. Some tested semen in dishes or straws, while animal studies irradiated testes or semen before insemination. The wide range and non-linear responses mean the studies do not identify one generally safe or optimal protocol.

Interpretation

The clearest repeated finding is that selected light exposures can alter sperm motility and energy-related measures in laboratory samples. Some livestock studies connect semen treatment with field fertility, but one large sow study was null and another reported breed-specific improvements. These are useful experimental and agricultural findings; they do not yet show that PBM improves fertility outcomes for people. Human trials should track fertilization, pregnancy, live birth, and offspring safety as well as semen parameters.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Many laboratory studies and a systematic review report higher motility under some red or near-infrared protocols, but responses vary with dose, storage, species, and light source, and one human-sperm study found cellular harm at its tested exposure. Livestock fertility findings do not establish human fertility benefit. Standardized safety studies and controlled human reproductive-outcome trials are needed.
